title: Why Every Christian Should Read Old Books
author: The Western Spirit
summary: The Western Spirit refutes the claim that Christianity destroyed classical civilization by tracing how the Church Fathers—Justin Martyr, Basil, Augustine—were themselves products of classical education who used pagan learning as a foundation for Christian thought. Augustine's conversion itself was sparked by reading Cicero; monasteries preserved the texts of Aristotle, Plato, Virgil, and Cicero when they might otherwise have been lost. Basil's Address to Young Men articulates the bee analogy: take from pagan writers what is true and useful, leave what is harmful. The article argues this posture—neither idolizing nor discarding classical texts—remains the best model for Christians engaging the Western canon today.
points: The claim that Christianity destroyed classical civilization is historically false: the Church Fathers were deeply formed by pagan learning before and after their conversions.
Augustine's Confessions records that reading Cicero's Hortensius—a pagan philosophical dialogue—was what awakened his hunger for wisdom and turned him toward God.
Monasteries served as the primary preservation mechanism for classical texts; without their scriptoria, works of Aristotle, Plato, Virgil, Tacitus, and Cicero might have been permanently lost.

Basil's bee analogy from his Address to Young Men provides the classical Christian reading method: take what is true and useful from pagan authors, leave what is harmful, and let the best serve the Gospel.
The Church Fathers modeled a posture of neither idolizing nor discarding the classical world—critical engagement that the piece argues remains the correct approach for Christians today.
quotes: St. Augustine spent years immersed in Cicero, Virgil, and the Latin classics before becoming one of Christianity's greatest theologians.

'This book of his contains an exhortation to philosophy...But this book altered my affections, and turned my prayers to Thyself, O Lord; and made me have other purposes and desires. Every vain hope at once became worthless to me; and I longed with an incredibly burning desire for an immortality of wisdom.'
Augustine eventually rejected Cicero's philosophy where it conflicted with Christianity, but he never rejected the pursuit of wisdom that Cicero had inspired.

Within their scriptoria, monks copied not only the Scriptures but also the writings of Aristotle, Plato, Virgil, Ovid, Livy, Tacitus, Cicero, and countless other authors whose works might otherwise have disappeared.

'Just as dyers prepare the cloth before they apply the dye...so indeed must we also, if we would preserve indelible the idea of the true virtue, become first initiated in the pagan lore, then at length give special heed to the sacred and divine teachings.'

The Church Fathers read the great books of the ancient world with open eyes and careful judgment. They neither idolized them nor discarded them. They received what was true, rejected what was false, and allowed the best of classical wisdom to serve the higher light of the Gospel.
